Summary: The paper builds a controlled benchmark for evidence-grounded knowledge-base writing from 100 OMIM phenotype entries. Each entry is drafted from its header and exactly the papers its curators cited (causal gene withheld), with one model (Claude Opus 5.5) doing all generation, claim-level auditing and judging, so that only the generation strategy varies. Strategies cover three paradigms (direct reading and an agentic curator; evidence graph and case-table-first extraction; recall-then-verify), a memory-only control and three add-ons (second-hand evidence, reconciled case database, learned curation guide). The primary endpoint is coverage of fixed fact lists (6,652 facts over 476 paragraphs) split once from OMIM allelic-variant descriptions as deposited in ClinVar. Main findings: hiding full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (paired +43.7, CI +38.3 to +49.1); on facts the supplied text states, three reading strategies convey 93.6-94.4% and on unstated facts 5.5-6.9%; direct reading, agentic curator and evidence graph are within about a point, case table first is behind (-1.9, larger on full-text-stated facts), and memory-based strategies convey far less. The paper also characterises what the audit can and cannot detect (planted single-value errors are caught; errors carried by second-hand passages are not), uses the memory-only control by creation date as a contamination check, and reports measurement lessons, notably that an asymmetric completion rule created a spurious 2.1-point difference.
Strengths: Unusually careful experimental control: same papers, same model, same guards, same audit and scoring across strategies, with fixed fact lists produced once without sight of any draft so all strategies share a denominator.

The within-paper access manipulation (hiding full text of the same 91 papers in 46 entries, no arm repaired) is a clean design that isolates input access from paper/entry identity, and the effect is large and well estimated.

Restricting the comparison to facts the supplied text states (Table 2) is a useful decomposition that separates 'how a strategy reads' from 'what it was given', and it makes the near-ceiling behaviour of the reading strategies visible.

Statistical reporting is honest and thorough: paired bootstrap intervals, better/worse/tied counts, sign tests, Holm correction for secondary measures, judge variation and run-to-run replicate noise (Appendix E), and an explicit example where the evidence graph flips sign across replicates.

Treating stopped (safety-filtered) replies as an outcome and showing that an asymmetric completion rule produced a spurious difference larger than the true between-strategy differences is a valuable, generalisable measurement lesson for agentic/pipeline evaluations.

The audit analysis is appropriately modest: the planted-error test is described as not a sensitivity estimate, and the second-hand-evidence analysis shows a concrete blind spot (fidelity to what the writer saw, not correctness).

Limitations are stated candidly and repeatedly (single model family, no human validation, narrow reference, given reference list), and the release plan (harness, drafts, verdicts, scores with fact IDs) supports reproducibility within licensing constraints.
Weaknesses: No human validation of any judgement. Fact splitting, present/absent judgements, the 'text states the fact' judgement on which Table 2 and Figure 3 rest, audit verdicts and variant-name matching are all made by the same model family that wrote the drafts. Given known self-preference effects (which the paper cites), even a small curator-annotated sample (e.g., 200-300 facts with inter-annotator agreement against the model) would substantially strengthen every headline number. As submitted, the central claims are measured only by model agreement with itself.

Single generator model. The headline conclusion ('what the strategy was given to read limits agreement far more than how it reads') is a claim about generation strategies in general but is established for one frontier model. With a weaker or smaller model the extract-then-write intermediates could plausibly matter much more; at least one other model family (even on a 30-entry subset) is needed before the conclusion can be generalised as the abstract and conclusion phrase it.

The main finding is largely expected, as the paper itself says: curators wrote from full papers, so drafts from abstracts convey less. The added value is the magnitude and the decomposition, but the magnitude is partly mechanical given that only 19% of papers have full text and the reference is variant-centred text that abstracts rarely contain. The 'stated facts' analysis then has a ceiling (95-97% on abstract-stated facts, most entries tied), which limits its power to discriminate strategies.

Narrow primary reference. Only about 24% of a direct-reading draft's statements have a counterpart in the reference paragraph, so the primary endpoint scores a minority of each draft; everything else is checked only by the same-model audit. Conclusions about which strategy writes better entries are therefore conclusions about variant-description recall, not about entry quality.

Between-strategy differences are within or near the replicate-noise scale (half-width 1.0 point over 93 entries) and the main comparison is a single run per entry. The paper is careful about this, but it means the comparative contribution reduces to 'three strategies are indistinguishable, one is slightly behind, partly due to implementation effort' (the matched ablation moves case table first from -2.3 to -0.2). The strategies are the authors' own implementations rather than published systems, so the comparison says little about existing systems.

Fit and generality for ICLR. The benchmark is tightly tied to OMIM/ClinVar/HPO and to given reference lists; retrieval is barely tested (ten entries), and inputs that do not fit one prompt are excluded. The paper argues that its measurement lessons generalise, but evidence for transfer beyond this domain is not presented. The scale (100 entries, 93 compared, 20 post-cutoff entries) is modest for a benchmark contribution.

Presentation is very dense. The main text packs many numbers, restrictions (pooled vs mean over entries, stated/partly stated, full-text/abstract/title) and caveats into short paragraphs, and many key definitions and results live in a long appendix (over 20 tables). Sections 4.4 and 4.7 in particular are hard to follow; the reader must track several different entry sets (93, 46, 49, 40/38, 30, 20, 68, 96). A summary table of entry sets in the main text and fewer inline numbers would help.

Contamination analysis is suggestive rather than conclusive: memory-only coverage is low for the newest entries, but the paper itself notes that within abstract-only papers direct-reading coverage declines with entry era, which is consistent with some memorisation contributing to reading results for older entries; this is not separated.
Questions: Can you provide any human validation, even small: e.g., a curator or domain expert labelling a random sample of fact statuses (present/partly/absent) and 'text states the fact' judgements, with agreement against the model? How would the headline numbers change under plausible judge error rates?
Have you run any strategy with a second model family (or a smaller model from the same family) on a subset? Does the closeness of the reading strategies hold when the writer is weaker?

How sensitive is the 'stated facts' result to the threshold for 'stated' versus 'partly stated'? What do the strategies convey on partly stated facts (1,198 facts), which seem to be where reading quality could matter most?

Given that the case-table deficit shrinks from -2.3 to -0.2 under matched extraction effort, is there any remaining evidence that the representation itself (rather than implementation effort) matters?
What is the 2.1-point spurious difference attributable to precisely: how many entries were excluded under the asymmetric rule, and were they systematically the entries where direct reading did well?

For the 24% of draft statements with a counterpart in the reference: how do strategies compare on the remaining 76% of content as judged by the audit, and is there any evidence the audit-judged supported rate tracks factual correctness?

Could you report results with the reference list partly corrupted or with retrieval on more than ten entries, to indicate how much the 'given exactly the cited papers' assumption drives the conclusions?
Limitations: Single model family for writing, auditing and judging, with no human validation; self-preference bias is acknowledged but unquantified.
Reference covers only variant-centred paragraphs and ontology annotations, a minority of each draft's content.
Strategies receive the curators' reference list; retrieval and long-input regimes are essentially untested.
Only open-access text without supplements; read versus recalled facts cannot be separated.
Strategies are the authors' own implementations developed on the main entry set; the clean 2026 set is small (20 entries).
The authors adequately acknowledge these limitations; a discussion of potential misuse (drafts presented as curated content) is present in the ethics statement.
Thought: Very carefully controlled and honestly reported evaluation; numbers are internally consistent (Fig 2/3 counts match text, Table 1/2 match prose, Fig 5 band sizes sum to 93). But the headline finding (access limits agreement) is acknowledged as expected, the strategy comparison yields mostly nulls at the noise scale with one gap largely explained by implementation effort, and everything rests on one model judging itself with zero human validation and a reference covering ~24% of draft content. For ICLR, a domain-specific benchmark with one model and no human grounding is below the bar despite the excellent measurement hygiene; a human-validated subset and a second model family would move this to accept territory. Leaning reject, persuadable.
